article_text:
As Muscat continues to develop and expand its cultural scene, Muscat Art returns for its fifth edition, presenting works by Omani and international artists under the theme Art Is Everywhere . Held at the Oman Convention and Exhibition Centre (OCEC) in partnership with BilArab Bin Haitham Initiatives, the event showcases art as a means of exploring identity and highlights the spaces that shape everyday life, while contributing to a wider conversation about the place of contemporary art within Oman’s cultural landscape.

Organised by OCEC, Muscat Art was established to provide a platform for artists to present their work and connect with a range of audiences. By drawing on Oman’s established artistic community while also creating opportunities for emerging artists, the exhibition serves as a meeting point that opens up possibilities for collaboration and the exchange of ideas. The 2026 edition features more than 300 participating artists, with Omani artist Anwar Sonya, a prominent figure in Oman’s contemporary art movement, amongst those showing work. The exhibition’s international dimension is reflected in its guest artists, among them Syrian artist Noor Bahjat, Fatma Lootah from the UAE, Palestinian artist Leen Al Ayoubi, Filipino artist Loriel Castillo, known as Yelcast, and Mustafa Suleiman . Their inclusion encourages a broader lens on artistic perspectives shaped by diverse cultural and personal experiences within a shared setting.

As its theme indicates, the exhibition looks beyond conventional artistic spaces to understand the ways in which we make sense of our environment. From architecture and inherited traditions to shared histories and everyday spaces, it encourages visitors to understand how creative practices are woven into the cultural fabric of a place, linking its heritage with contemporary perspectives. A diverse events programme enriches the exhibition through a series of activations including workshops, art talks and panel discussions, enabling an audience experience that extends beyond simply viewing the artworks. The workshops will invite participants to engage with different artistic techniques and media, while the Art Talks – entitled Reimagining Space: Artists Reshaping Places, Ideas, and Traditions – will address how artists respond to the environments and contexts around them. Complementing these conversations will be a series of panel discussions considering the evolving creative industries and the relationship between artistic expression, entrepreneurship and cultural development.

An annual exhibition such as Art Is Everywhere offers a stimulating and rewarding encounter, but its wider significance lies in its layered contribution to the wider scene. For Muscat Art, presenting more than 300 artists from different backgrounds creates an opportunity to strengthen relationships between local and international creative communities. It serves a space through which contemporary art practitioners can gain greater visibility and where the ‘art conversation’ is strengthened and diversified. While history and tradition remain integral to Oman’s identity, artists continue to find innovative ways of interpreting these references in dialogue with the present. These ambitions sit within a broader conversation about the development of the country’s cultural sector. As Muscat continues to expand its arts scene, the involvement of cultural and tourism institutions also point to an understanding of art as part of the Sultanate’s larger cultural offering and the potential to attract visitors to experiences that reach beyond conventional sightseeing.

Muscat Art 2026 is presented by BilArab Bin Haitham Initiatives as the Lead Sponsor, with the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Youth and the Ministry of Heritage and Tourism serving as Strategic Partners. Sadolin also supports the exhibition as the Colour Sponsor and Omq Production as the Creative Partner.

Muscat Art 2026 runs from 28 until 30 October

解説・あらすじ

金子正次が脚本・主演を務めた1983年公開の大ヒット映画「竜二」を、柳楽優弥が主演を務めてリメイク。「舞妓Haaaan!!!」「謝罪の王様」などの水田伸生監督がメガホンをとり、裏社会に生きながらも愛する家族を守ろうともがく男の姿を、現代的なリアリティとともに描き出す。 昭和59年から平成2年にかけての新宿・歌舞伎町。腕っぷしが強く情に厚いヤクザの竜二は、舎弟の直とひろしを家族のように愛していた。やがてまり子と出会い息子が生まれた彼は、家族を守るために裏社会から足を洗うことを決意し、酒屋の配達員として懸命に働きはじめる。生活は決して楽ではないが、自らが望んだ穏やかな暮らしを手に入れたはずだった。しかし、薬物に溺れた兄弟分のカズや、竜二にとってもうひとつの家族である舎弟たちとの再会が、彼を過去へと引き戻していく。 竜二が愛する女性・まり子を川栄李奈、舎弟の直を萩原利久、もう1人の舎弟・ひろしをダンス＆ボーカルグループ「BE:FIRST」のJUNON、兄弟分のカズを三宅健、竜二が所属する組の幹部・新田を伊藤英明、竜二に因縁を抱える敵対組織の宮内をダンス＆ボーカルグループ「MAZZEL」のRYUKIが演じる。「BE:FIRST」が主題歌を担当し、JUNONが作詞・作曲にも参加した。

article_text:
Much of the discussion around the 2027 Sundance Film Festival has understandably focused on the festival’s move to Boulder, Colorado , from its longtime home in Park City. But with less than three months until the festival starts , it’s finally time to start discussing some films.

Sundance has announced its first wave of Legacy programming, which will screen restorations of influential films from the festival’s history in a section co-presented by Letterboxd. Highlights include Alfonso Cuarón’s “Y Tu Mamá También,” Julie Taymor’s “Fool’s Fire,” and Barbara Hammer’s landmark documentary “Nitrate Kisses,” all celebrating notable anniversaries in 2027.

The festival will also host a special “Cinema Interruptus” screening of Christopher Nolan’s “Memento,” a University of Colorado tradition in which audience members can pause the film at any time to ask a question or spark a discussion.

“We’re excited to kick off the Festival season in earnest with this first 2027 Sundance Film Festival announcement, revealing some of our Legacy programming,” said Sundance Film Festival director Eugene Hernandez said in a statement. “Each year we honor the legacy of our founder Robert Redford and the history of the Sundance Film Festival by looking back at just a few of the films and filmmakers who have shaped our history. Our first festival in our new home in Boulder, Colorado will bring change, but as we evolve, we’ll keep at our core what we celebrate: our rich history. Sundance will always uplift independent voices, and our Legacy slate is a beautiful example of that. We are also pleased to announce Letterboxd’s co-partnership for the Legacy category — it’s great to collaborate with organizations that build momentum and excitement for a culture of cinematic discovery, and we look forward to having them at the Festival with us in January.”

The 2027 Sundance Film Festival runs from January 21-31, 2027 in Boulder, Colorado. Keep reading for the full list of announced Legacy programming, with descriptions from Sundance

“ Better Luck Tomorrow” / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Justin Lin, Screenwriters: Ernesto Foronda, Fabian Marquez, Producers: Julie Asato, Ernesto Foronda) — To escape the crushing pressure of academic perfection, a group of high-achieving teens lead a secret, thrill-seeking double life of petty crime that quickly spins out of control. Cast: Karin Anna Cheung, John Cho, Roger Fan, Sung Kang, Parry Shen, Jason Tobin. Fiction. 25th anniversary. Better Luck Tomorrow premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. It was subsequently released with small changes in the edit. The original 2002 Sundance Film Festival cut of Better Luck Tomorrow was restored by the UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Sundance Institute and Perfect Storm Entertainment, with funding provided by Chris Quintos Cathcart, co-CEO of Unapologetic Projects. The 4K restoration utilized the original 35 mm camera negatives, 35 mm Sundance Film Festival print, and DA-88 sound materials and was supervised by filmmaker Justin Lin at Resillion and Deluxe Audio Services. Additional lab services by Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. The release version has also been restored and archived. Special thanks to Paramount Pictures for permission to screen the film.

“Dogtown and Z-Boys “ / U.S.A (Director and Screenwriter: Stacy Peralta, Screenwriter: Craig Stecyk, Producer: Agi Orsi) — The Z-Boys: outcast surf rats from the run-down Dogtown neighborhood in Venice, California, who revolutionized skateboarding with their innovative style and attitude. An exploration of the birth of a cultural phenomenon, narrated by Sean Penn and featuring old-school skating footage, a blistering soundtrack, and interviews with Tony Alva, Jay Adams, and Tony Hawk. Documentary. 25th Anniversary of U.S. Release. Dogtown and Z-Boys premiered at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition and won the Audience Award: Documentary and Directing Award: Documentary. 2027 marks the 25th anniversary of its theatrical release. The 4K digital restoration was undertaken from the original 35 mm elements by Sony Pictures Classics. The restoration was approved by the filmmakers.

“Fool’s Fire “ / U.S.A. (Director, Screenwriter, and Producer: Julie Taymor, Producer: Kerry Orent) — A captured dwarf, Hopfrog, is forced to become jester to a tyrannical king. But when the King is gifted with another little person, whom the king debases and shames, Hopfrog plots a terrible revenge. Based on the story “Hop-Frog” by Edgar Allan Poe. Cast: Michael J. Anderson, Tom Hewitt, Mireille Mossé. Fiction. 35th anniversary. Fool’s Fire premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition. This new restoration was created by the nonprofit IndieCollect in collaboration with Julie Taymor and with support from the Golden Globe Foundation, using a 6.5K scan of the original 35 mm negative and a soundtrack restored by Endpoint Audio Labs from the optical track negative. Featuring an extended conversation with Julie Taymor and clips from The Making of Fool’s Fire , exploring the film’s artistry and cutting-edge use of high definition.

“Nitrate Kisses “ / U.S.A. (Director: Barbara Hammer) — A liberating portrait of queer sexuality that weaves striking images of four lesbian and gay couples with archival footage, interviews, sexual imagery, and queer cinema dating back to the 1930s to unearth forbidden and long-invisible histories. Documentary. Nitrate Kisses had its U.S. premiere at the 1993 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Documentary Competition. Nitrate Kisses was preserved by the Academy Film Archive. The original 16 mm A/B-rolls were scanned at 4K and restored by BB Optics. The mono mix was digitized from the original 16 mm mag track. The restoration was funded by Frameline and supervised by The Estate of Barbara Hammer and Brydie O’Connor.

“Real Women Have Curves “ / U.S.A. (Director: Patricia Cardoso, Screenwriters: George LaVoo, Josefina López, Producers: George Lavoo, Effie Brown) — Ana, a first-generation Mexican American teenager, fights for her independence and her curves in a war of wills with her mother. Based on the play by Josefina López. Cast: America Ferrera, George Lopez, Ingrid Oliu, Lupe Ontiveros, Brian Sites. Fiction. 25th anniversary. Real Women Have Curves premiered at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Audience Award: Dramatic and the Special Jury Prize for Acting for America Ferrera and Lupe Ontiveros. Supervised by director Patricia Cardoso and director of photography Jim Denault, this new 4K restoration was undertaken by Criterion in collaboration with Warner Bros. Pictures, Sundance Institute, and the Academy Film Archive from the 35 mm original camera negative.

“Swoon “ / U.S.A. (Director and Screenwriter: Tom Kalin, Producers: Christine Vachon) — The true story of Nathan Leopold and Richard Loeb, who kidnapped and brutally murdered 14-year-old Bobby Franks in Chicago in 1924. The revelation that these wealthy Jewish college students had a sexual relationship scandalized the nation. After their arrest and trial, they were sentenced to life plus 99 years. Cast: Craig Chester, Michael Kirby, John A. Mudd, Daniel Schlachet, Natalie Stanford, Michael Stumm, Ron Vawter. Fiction. 35th anniversary. Swoon premiered at the 1992 Sundance Film Festival as part of the U.S. Dramatic Competition and took home the Excellence in Cinematography Award: Dramatic. Swoon was restored by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive in collaboration with Frameline, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute in 4K from the original 16 mm A/B camera negatives, 35 mm interpositive, 35 mm dupe negative, and 35 mm magnetic track. The restoration was supervised by Tom Kalin and Ellen Kuras at Roundabout Entertainment, Inc. and Deluxe Audio Services. Restoration funding was provided by the Academy Film Archive and UCLA Film & Television Archive with additional support from Frameline, Ellen Kuras, Strand Releasing, and Sundance Institute.

“Y tu mamá también “ / Mexico (Director, Screenwriter and Producer: Alfonso Cuarón, Screenwriter: Carlos Cuarón, Producer: Jorge Vergara) — After their girlfriends jet off for the summer, a pair of Mexico City teenagers become bewitched by an older Spanish woman they meet at a wedding. When she agrees to accompany them on a road trip, the three form an increasingly intense and sensual bond. Cast: Gael García Bernal, Diego Luna, Maribel Verdú. Fiction. 25th anniversary. Y tu mamá también screened at the 2002 Sundance Film Festival as part of the Special Events category. Newly restored by Esperanto Films in 4K under the supervision of filmmaker Alfonso Cuarón and cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki. A Janus Films release.

Sundance Film Festival presents: Cinema Interruptus featuring “Memento” A unique tradition established at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Conference on World Affairs (CWA) by film critic Roger Ebert and CWA founder and sociology professor Howard Higman, Cinema Interruptus is communal film criticism in two sessions. As “Memento” screens, participants can yell “Stop!” at any point to make a comment or ask a question, after which the film will resume. Critic and author Josh Larsen — who hosted Interruptus at CWA on campus from 2017 to 2024 — will moderate the discussion and keep things on track, with the goal of finishing the entire movie by the end of the second session.

“ Memento” / U.S.A. (Director: Christopher Nolan) — A former insurance investigator who now suffers from anterograde amnesia uses notes and tattoos to hunt down his wife’s murderer. Fiction.

“Memento” had its U.S. festival premiere at the 2001 Sundance Film Festival in the U.S. Dramatic Competition and it took home the Waldo Salt Screenwriting Award. Restored in 4K from original interpositive materials by Umbrella with approval from director Christopher Nolan. Cinema Interruptus is also part of our Offscreen program, to be announced in its entirety soon.

article_text:
千葉県立美術館（千葉市中央区）で、「大チーバくん展―さかざきちはるとチーバくんの20年」が10月31日から開催されます。

県と県民の方をつなぐキャラクターとしてのチーバくんと、さかざきちはるさんの描くオリジナルなチーバくん。2つのスタイルを有するチーバくんの20年のあゆみと未来へとつながる世界観を見ることができます。

大チーバくん展―さかざきちはるとチーバくんの20年

会場：千葉県立美術館（千葉県千葉市中央区中央港1-10-1）

会期：2026年10月31日（土）～2027年1月17日（日）

開館時間：9:00～16:30（入場は16:00まで）

休館日：月曜日（ただし11/23、1/11は開館）、11/24（火）、12/28（月）から1/4（月）、1/12（火）

入館料：一般1,000円、高校・大学生500円 ※中学生以下、65歳以上、障害者手帳等をお持ちの方とその介護者1名は無料 ※11/3（火・祝）文化の日は、どなたでも無料

アクセス： 電車・モノレール：JR京葉線または千葉都市モノレール「千葉みなと」駅下車徒歩約10分 自動車：東京方面から東関東自動車道「湾岸習志野」I.C.、成田方面から京葉道路「穴川」I.C.、東金方面から千葉東金道路「千葉東」I.C.、館山方面から京葉道路「松ヶ丘」I.C.からそれぞれ約20分 ※駐車場無料（78台うち2台障害者用）

詳細は、 千葉県立美術館公式サイト まで。

展示概要

県と県民をつなぐチーバくん

千葉県の形から生まれたチーバくん。その姿を見ない日はないほど、千葉の暮らしの中に浸透しています。県の推進する事業を盛り上げるために制作されたロゴマークなど、さかざきちはるさんが手がけてきたアートワークを全て見ることができます。

チーバくんについて 千葉県に住む不思議ないきもの。好奇心旺盛でいろいろなことに挑戦するのが大好き。未知のものに立ち向かうときほど勇気と情熱がわき、からだが赤く輝く。食いしん坊でいたずら好きな面も。横から見た姿が千葉県の形をしています。

さかざきちはるさんの描くオリジナルなチーバくん

二曲一双屏風絵《まねきチーバくん「開運招福」》 横幅2メートル、高さ1.5メートルの超大作原画作品。〈開運〉〈招福〉それぞれの小判を手に持った「まねきチーバくん」が対で描き下ろしされます。千葉県松戸市に本社を持ち、地域産材を活用した建具・遊具作りで知られる山二建具さんによる、美しい屏風の設えとともにお楽しみください。

チーバくんと日本の仲間たちパズル さかざきちはるさんによって、全都道府県にチーバくんの目と鼻と口が描き加えられた日本地図。これを木製のパズルとして製作、展示されます。展示作品とは別に、実際に手に取って遊ぶことのできるパズルも準備する予定です。パズル製作：山二建具

絵本『チーバくんのあいうえお』 さかざきちはるさんが、初めてチーバくんを主人公にして制作した絵本『チーバくんのあいうえお』（ペンギンデザイン刊）が本展開幕に合わせて発売されます。本展では、チーバくんと一緒に「あいうえお」をめぐる本作の「あ」～「ん」までのすべてのページが公開されます。

あかいチーバくんがあかいものあつめるあいうえおの本です。まずはあいうえお順にあかいものを探すことから始めていちご いっぱい チーバくんすいかすきすき チーバくんのようにあたまの文字が重なる文章をつくりました。それから文章からイメージできる場面や組み合わせをどんどん描いていきました。えびとえびぞり チーバくんたことたたかう チーバくんのように今までにないポーズのチーバくんがたくさん生まれました。（あとがきより）

さかざきちはるさんのおしごと

Suicaのペンギンをはじめとする、これまでに生み出された魅力的なキャラクターも展示。絵本作家としての一面にも注目し、その創作活動や作品が紹介されます。

さかざきちはる 作家プロフィール

絵本作家・イラストレーター。1967年千葉県市川市に生まれる。1991年東京藝術大学美術学部デザイン科卒業。1991年ステーショナリーメーカーにデザイナーとして勤務。1998年に独立。イラストレーター、絵本作家として活動を続ける。2001年「Suicaのペンギン」（JR東日本）、2007年「チーバくん」（千葉県）、など数多くのキャラクターデザインを手がける。近年はペンギンをモチーフにした絵画、版画などの作品展を日本各地で開いている。2024年佐賀県嬉野温泉の和多屋別荘内に原画500点を収蔵した「Penguin Museum」が誕生。

誕生から20年という節目を迎え、千葉県のシンボルとして世代を超えて愛され続けているチーバくん。本展は、公的マスコットとしての日々のアートワークから、さかざきちはるさんの自由で温かな感性が息づくオリジナル原画まで、その多面的な魅力をたっぷりと体感できる貴重な機会です。会場を包むユニークなダンボール空間や、ここでしか出合えない限定グッズが並ぶ特別なショップなど、大人から子どもまで誰もが笑顔になれる仕掛けにも要注目です。愛らしくも奥深いチーバくんの豊かな世界へ、ぜひ足を運んでみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

In her new book, “ Hollywood Whispers : The Untold Story of the Original Gossip Queens, Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper ,” Eileen Cope delves into a rivalry that dramatically shaped the entertainment industry and culture at large throughout the mid-20th century. After the birth of the star system in Hollywood, Parsons and Hopper rose to prominence as gossip columnists who could make and break careers, and choose to keep or expose celebrities’ secrets. With a combined readership of 75 million at their peak, Hopper and Parsons wielded extraordinary influence — and instilled paralyzing fear. As columnist Liz Smith has written, “The studios created both of them. And they thought they could control both of them. But they became Frankenstein monsters escaped from the labs.” In the excerpt below, Cope summarizes their stark differences — and even more striking similarities.

Hollywood has always been a hall of mirrors. What began as an industry of light and illusion had, by the 1940s, become a machinery of control—an empire built on fantasy, running on fear. Its dreammakers no longer needed scripts or cameras to keep order. They had Louella Parsons and Hedda Hopper.

By then, both women had transcended the ordinary limits of journalism. They were not simply reporters; they were gatekeepers of belief, the quiet regulators of a nation’s imagination. To cross them was to risk vanishing—not merely from the screen, but from the collective story America told about itself.

Hollywood insiders referred to them—half jokingly, half in dread—as “the High Priestesses.” Studio secretaries clipped their columns before the morning dailies reached the lot, marking any mention of the studio’s stars with red pencil. Publicists phoned assistants in panic if a name appeared in the wrong context. “They could wreck you before lunch,” remembered producer Pandro Berman. “And by dinner, they’d make you again—if it suited them.”

It was easy, at first, to mistake their power for personality. Louella, with her sanctimonious charm and the backing of William Randolph Hearst, ruled the studios from her desk at the Los Angeles Examiner. Her typewriter was a throne. Her column ran like clockwork through America’s breakfast tables, a sermon of what was right and who had sinned. Hedda, the actress-turned-crusader, cultivated a different tone—brassy, righteous, vengeful. Her voice carried across radio waves like a call to arms. She didn’t just write gossip; she announced it, her cadence turning every name into an accusation or an absolution.

Both women understood theater. Louella played the role of moral mother, her column written in the soothing cadences of propriety—rarely venomous on the surface, yet devastating in its implications. Hedda was the showwoman. “When she walked into Ciro’s,” recalled gossip photographer Frank Worth, “it was like someone had switched on the lights.” Even those who loathed her found themselves glancing up, afraid she might be looking at them.

Louella and Hedda were two sides of the same coin, minted in a culture that worshipped celebrity and feared moral chaos. Each understood what the studios feared most: scandal, exposure, the sudden rupture of the illusion. And they learned to trade in that fear, turning rumor into regulation.

Louella had built her empire first. By the early 1930s, her column appeared in hundreds of newspapers through the Hearst syndicate, reaching an estimated twenty million readers daily. Hollywood Hotel, her weekly radio show, brought the glamour of opening nights directly into American living rooms. Its mix of studio orchestras, star appearances, and previews of upcoming films created a powerful cycle of cross-promotion: her print column drove listeners to the broadcast, and the broadcast reinforced her authority in print.

She was feared as much as courted. Stars who crossed her found themselves frozen out. Studio executives who annoyed her might find their films receiving tepid coverage. A single line hinting that an actor appeared “unhappy with recent assignments” could trigger studio meetings and contract reviews. Louella’s prose was brief, polite, and devastatingly coded; her readers learned to interpret her tone as carefully as her text. The fear she inspired was not only of what she printed but of what she might choose not to.

The competition she could not have predicted came in the form of a woman she had once treated as a harmless curiosity. By 1935, Hedda Hopper’s film career was essentially over. She was fifty, though she claimed forty-five, watching her savings evaporate and terrified about her future. When a studio executive suggested she could “transition to extra work,” Hedda turned the humiliation into fuel. If she couldn’t star in movies, she would make herself the story. The weapon she would wield was not beauty or youth, but the pen.

When a friend suggested she try writing a gossip column, Hedda was insulted. Writing gossip seemed like a public acknowledgment that she couldn’t make it as a performer. But desperation has a way of making humiliation seem acceptable. She borrowed a typewriter, set up at her kitchen table, and began by writing what she knew best: the petty rivalries of actors who had underestimated her. “I never lied,” she said later, “but I didn’t always tell the truth either.” The early columns were messy but alive, full of energy and vengeance.

Then Hedda got angry. She stopped trying to write like a journalist and started writing like herself— sharp, critical, unsparing, willing to say things other columnists wouldn’t dare print. Twenty years as a working actress had also given her something valuable: relationships with the people Louella ignored. Character actors, crew members, hairdressers, chauffeurs, and wardrobe girls had no loyalty to Louella, and many were happy to talk to Hedda, who had once been one of them.

The Los Angeles Times noticed. Hearst’s primary competitor in Southern California saw Hedda as a weapon against his dominance through Louella. In 1938, the paper offered Hedda a contract with better pay, more resources, and a much larger platform. She would compete directly with the woman who had been Hollywood’s undisputed gossip queen for fifteen years.

Most people thought she would be crushed. Instead, Hedda transformed herself for the opportunity. She began wearing the enormous hats that became her trademark—creations decorated with feathers, flowers, fruit, and even stuffed animals. The hats ensured that everyone at a Hollywood event knew when Hedda Hopper had arrived. She also developed a confrontational style that contrasted with Louella’s cozy approach. Where Louella praised, Hedda criticized. Where Louella protected relationships, Hedda burned bridges. Where Louella sought to be loved, Hedda was content to be feared.

In the beginning, the difference between them seemed simple enough. Louella had the empire; Hedda had the instinct. Louella’s authority came from her link to Hearst—a patriarchal structure she both served and mastered. Hedda’s came from sheer velocity. She moved fast, wrote fast, spoke fast. She had learned that outrage was more contagious than affection.

At first, the two women coexisted uneasily, even politely. Louella sent Hedda a congratulatory telegram when her first radio broadcast went national. Hedda responded with a bouquet of orchids and a note that read, “To the Queen of the Kingdom I am only visiting.” But the civility evaporated as soon as Hedda’s column began pulling readers away from the Examiner. In 1940, when Hedda’s column syndication reached more than six million households, Louella persuaded Hearst’s editors to bar her rival from every Hearst-owned paper.

As the 1940s unfolded, their feud became public theater. Columns answered columns. Louella hinted that Hedda was “overly dramatic.” Hedda fired back, calling Louella “a relic of studio servitude.” Studios courted both women, sometimes feeding them different versions of the same story to see who would publish first. Readers began to choose sides.

In 1945, Photoplay published “Battle of the Typewriters,” complete with caricatures of the two women as dueling queens—Louella seated on a gilt throne, Hedda brandishing her hatpins like weapons. The story outsold every issue that year except the one featuring Clark Gable’s return from the war. The public couldn’t get enough. For a nation recovering from global conflict, the spectacle of two powerful women waging a cold war of words was irresistible.

Their methods echo through the media that followed. The tabloid boom of the 1980s, TMZ, Instagram, celebrity influencers, blind-item accounts, and the daily social-media outrage cycle all trace their lineage to the template Louella and Hedda built. They understood that access could be traded, intimacy manufactured, morality weaponized, and a public image constructed or destroyed through repetition. The machine they built continues to hum behind every red carpet and every scandal recycled for entertainment. What they truly enshrined was attention—and America never stopped worshiping it.

The women themselves could not stop Hollywood from moving on. As the studio system declined and stars emerged, the two gossip queens became relics of the world they had once governed. When the Los Angeles Examiner folded in 1962, Louella suffered a professional blow. Already showing signs of physical deterioration, she nevertheless continued going out, bejeweled and bewildered, like a dowager empress whose country had overthrown her rule. She finally retired in 1965, beset by further medical problems.

Hedda had always advised leaving a party before the glow faded. On February 1, 1966, she died in Los Angeles of double pneumonia at the age of eighty. Her cryptic parting words were entirely in character: “They should know what I haven’t written!”

Louella’s daughter, Harriet, visited her mother at the Santa Monica nursing home to deliver the news that Hedda Hopper was dead. Louella sat in profound silence, then appeared confused. She would live for another six years, largely withdrawn from the world she had once ruled, before dying of arteriosclerosis on December 9, 1972, at the age of ninety-one. But on hearing that her great rival had finally departed, Louella gathered herself long enough to offer one last, unmistakable verdict: “GOOD!”

article_text:
Daily Capital , a new fund focused on Taiwan -Japan film and television co-productions, launched on the Tokyo International Film Festival market TIFFCOM ’s opening day at the “Taiwan Originals: Project Showcase” event.

The fund aims to raise NT$100 million (about $3.1 million) and invest in at least five projects across film, television and animation over its first two years. Fundraising has reached 70% of the target, and the fund expects to begin operations by year-end, founder Chang Chen-yu told Variety .

Related Stories

Netflix Touts International Success Amid Content Leadership Shake-Up, Eyes More Broadcaster Deals After TF1 and Globo Pacts

The name “Daily” reflects the idea that meaningful progress is built through daily efforts, Chang said at the launch.

In Japan, Daily Capital has identified K2 Pictures and Remow as co-development partners. Founded by producer Kii Muneyuki, K2 Pictures brings together Japanese filmmakers including Iwai Shunji, Miike Takashi, Nishikawa Miwa and Kore-eda Hirokazu. Remow is backed by Japanese entertainment and media companies including Shueisha, Toei, Amuse, Shochiku, TBS Holdings and Fuji Media Holdings, with access to established IP libraries and distribution networks.

“Investment amounts will vary according to each project’s scale and needs, whether it’s a film, series or animation. We expect to come in during development or pre-production, contribute to script discussions and help assemble the core creative team. We also aim to keep the primary capital recovery period within three years,” Chang said.

The fund plans to pair Japan’s IP and production know-how with Taiwan’s flexible financing and co-production experience. It will also tap local production incentives and distribution networks to reach audiences beyond Japanese- and Mandarin-speaking markets.

Its first announced investment is the series “Love Ends in Bloom.” Set in 1930s Chiayi and Alishan, the 10-episode historical romance and business drama follows a Japanese geisha who devises a cross-border marriage scheme to save her mother, then falls into a forbidden romance with a Taiwanese timber magnate. The story unfolds during the Japanese colonial period (1895–1945), when Taiwan’s cypress industry was thriving, and views the era through a Japanese woman’s eyes.

The project grew out of Chang’s return to his hometown of Chiayi in 2023. The railway station was under renovation, prompting him to reflect on the city’s forestry and railway history. “Despite our proximity, Taiwan, Japan and Korea are rarely seen together in one narrative,” Chang said in a previous interview with Variety .

Written by Juliana Hsu, whose credits include period drama “Gold Leaf,” and directed by Sun Jie-heng, director of wartime historical drama “Three Tears in Borneo,” “Love Ends in Bloom” is slated to begin filming in February 2027, targeting a mid-2028 release.

“The fund will measure success by whether its projects reach Japanese broadcasters, regional platforms and global streamers, and meet projected returns,” Chang said. “Those results could help Daily Capital raise a larger second fund focused on Taiwan-Japan and wider Asian co-productions.”

editorial_excerpt_zh: 徕卡相机股份公司（Leica Camera AG）将 2026 年度徕卡名人堂奖授予墨西哥摄影师 Graciela Iturbide，以表彰其成就。她是世界上的 […] 这篇文章 Graciela Iturbide is to receive the 2026 Leica Hall of Fame Award 最初发表于 The Eye of Photography…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "徕卡相机股份公司（Leica Camera AG）将 2026 年度徕卡名人堂奖授予墨西哥摄影师 Graciela Iturbide，以表彰其成就。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "她是当今世界最著名的墨西哥摄影师：今年，Graciela Iturbide 荣获“徕卡名人堂”奖，以表彰其一生的艺术成就。颁奖典礼于 2026 年 8 月 8 日在韦茨拉尔（Wetzlar）的徕卡世界（Leica World）举行的“摄影庆典”（Celebration of Photography）期间举行。配套展览展出了 50 多幅摄影作品，将在韦茨拉尔的徕卡画廊（Leica Gallery）展出至 2027 年 1 月。Iturbide 拍摄于 1986 年墨西哥瓦哈卡州（Oaxaca）“胡奇坦”（Juchitán）系列的摄影作品《Na’ Lupe Pan》被评为“2026 年度徕卡照片”。该展览深入呈现了这位艺术家的创作，其作品主要聚焦于拉丁美洲的文化历史。Iturbide 的视觉世界探索了生死、仪式和日常生活等普世主题，具有动人的诗意和魔幻色彩。这位摄影师突出了文化与自然、传统与现代、身份与表征之间的张力，使她的影像保留了一种神秘莫测的多义性。深根于墨西哥本土文化，并将超现实主义元素与宗教和神秘主义相融合，Graciela Iturbide 在几十年间发展出了一种独一无二的视觉语言——主要以黑白为主。鸟类和面具作为象征性的伴侣屡屡出现。这位摄影师最著名的作品是令人惊叹的《鬣蜥圣母》（Nuestra Señora de las iguanas / Our Lady of the Iguanas），拍摄于 1979 年胡奇坦的一个市场上。这是一个神秘的肖像，展现了一位头戴活鬣蜥王冠的女摊贩：她既是一个墨西哥式的九头蛇，又根据基督教的诠释，成了一个戴着荆棘冠冕、具有动物特性的女性基督形象。Graciela Iturbide 的摄影作品属于融合了心理与精神元素的人文主义传统，将纪实影像转化为一种极具细微差别的、高度主观的摄影形式。除了静物和风景之外，她关于墨西哥原住民社区生活条件以及母系社会结构重要性的社会纪实报道也轰动一时，确立了她作为拉丁美洲最重要的摄影之声之一的地位。为配合徕卡名人堂奖的颁发而举办的展览汇集了来自五个系列的 50 多幅照片：“胡奇坦”（Juchitán），展出了这位墨西哥瓦哈卡州城市从 1979 年至 1988 年的影像；《经典墨西哥》（México Clásicas，1974–2008）；《鸟类》（Pájaros，1987–1998）、《索诺拉沙漠》（Desierto de Sonora，1979）以及在厄瓜多尔、巴拿马、阿根廷和古巴拍摄的《旅行》（Viajes，1972–1994）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "格拉谢拉·伊图尔比德（Graciela Iturbide）于1942年5月16日出生于墨西哥城。早在孩童时期，她就对摄影着迷：她的父亲是一位热心的业余摄影爱好者。19岁时，她与建筑师曼努埃尔·罗查·迪亚斯（Manuel Rocha Díaz，1936–1996）结婚，并育有三个孩子。1969年，她开始在墨西哥国家学院的电影大学研究中心（CUEC）学习电影。1970年，她担任摄影师曼努埃尔·阿尔瓦雷斯·布拉沃（Manuel Álvarez Bravo）的助手一年，陪同他进行了多次旅行，从而发现了乡村墨西哥及其原住民社区的多样性。命运的转折——她六岁女儿克劳迪娅（Cláudia）的离世——彻底改变了格拉谢拉·伊图尔比德的生活，促使她决定成为一名职业摄影师。1975年，她在墨西哥城举办了她的首场展览，随后于1976年在纽约举办了首展。自20世纪80年代起，她开始获得国际认可。她曾获得众多奖项，包括W·尤金·史密斯奖（1987年）、雨果·埃尔夫特奖（1989年）、阿尔勒国际摄影节奖（1991年）、哈苏奖（2008年）、墨西哥城国家美术与文学研究所（INBAL）金奖（2024年）以及阿斯图里亚斯公主艺术奖（2025年）。伊图尔比德现居墨西哥城。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Leica Camera AG honours the Mexican photographer Graciela Iturbide by presenting her with the 2026 Leica Hall of Fame Award.

She is the world’s most famous contemporary Mexican photographer: this year, Graciela Iturbide was awarded the ‘Leica Hall of Fame’ prize in recognition of her life’s work. The award ceremony took place as part of the ‘Celebration of Photography’ on 8 October 2026 at Leica World in Wetzlar. The accompanying exhibition, featuring more than 50 photographs, will be on display at the Leica Gallery in Wetzlar until January 2027. Iturbide’s photograph ‘Na’ Lupe Pan’, from the series ‘Juchitán’, Oaxaca, Mexico, 1986, was voted ‘Leica Photo of the Year 2026’. The exhibition offers an in-depth insight into the artist’s work, which is primarily devoted to Latin American cultural history. Exploring universal themes such as life and death, rituals and everyday experiences, Iturbide’s visual world is characterised by its moving poetry and magic. The photographer highlights the tensions between culture and nature, tradition and modernity, identity and representation, ensuring that her images retain an enigmatic ambiguity. Deeply rooted in indigenous Mexican culture and blending surrealist elements with religion and mysticism, Graciela Iturbide has, over many decades, developed an inimitable visual language – predominantly in black and white. Birds and masks appear time and again as symbolic companions. The photographer’s most famous work, the astonishing ‘Nuestra Señora de las iguanas’ (Our Lady of the Iguanas), was taken in 1979 at a market in Juchitán. It is a mysterious portrait of a market vendor wearing a crown of live iguanas: a Mexican hydra, but also, according to Christian interpretation, a female figure of Christ wearing a crown of thorns with an animalistic character. Graciela Iturbide’s photographic work is part of a humanist tradition that incorporates psychological and spiritual elements, transforming the documentary image into a form of subjective photography that is extraordinarily rich in nuance. In addition to her still lifes and landscapes, it is her social reportage on the living conditions of Mexico’s indigenous communities and on the importance of matriarchal social structures that has caused a sensation and established her as one of Latin America’s most important photographic voices. The exhibition, organised to coincide with the presentation of the Leica Hall of Fame Award, brings together more than 50 photographs from five series: ‘Juchitán’, featuring images of this Mexican city in the state of Oaxaca (1979–1988); ‘México Clásicas’ (1974–2008); ‘Pájaros ’ (Birds, 1987–1998), ‘Desierto de Sonora’ (1979) and ‘Viajes’ (Travels), taken in Ecuador, Panama, Argentina and Cuba (1972–1994).

Graciela Iturbide was born in Mexico City on 16 May 1942. Even as a child, she was fascinated by photography: her father was a keen amateur photographer. She married the architect Manuel Rocha Díaz (1936–1996) at the age of 19 and went on to have three children. In 1969, she began studying film at the Colegio Nacional de México, at the Centro Universitario de Estudios Cinematográficos (CUEC). In 1970, she spent a year as an assistant to the photographer Manuel Álvarez Bravo, accompanying him on numerous trips and thereby discovering rural Mexico and the diversity of its indigenous communities. A twist of fate – the death of her six-year-old daughter Cláudia – radically changed Graciela Iturbide’s life, leading her to decide to become a professional photographer. In 1975, she held her first exhibition in Mexico City, followed by her first in New York in 1976. From the 1980s onwards, she began to gain international recognition. She has received numerous awards, including the W. Eugene Smith Prize (1987), the Hugo Erfurth Prize (1989), the Rencontres Internationales de la Photographie d’Arles Prize (1991), the Hasselblad Award (2008), the Gold Medal from the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL) in Mexico City (2024) and the Princess of Asturias Award for the Arts (2025). Iturbide lives in Mexico City.

article_text:
Sir Patrick Stewart , the beloved stage and screen star known for his role as Jean-Luc Picard in “ Star Trek : The Next Generation,” has died at the age of 86 years old. News of his death was first reported by The New York Times .

A fixture of the stage and screen for the past six decades, Stewart was equally active in the realms of classical drama and contemporary genre entertainment. Born in Mirfield, England in 1940, Stewart attended the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and began acting with the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966. He remained a member through 1982, playing many of the Bard’s most iconic roles and becoming a fixture of British television. It would have already been enough to call his acting career a successful one, but Hollywood stardom came calling for him in the late ’80s.

In 1987, Stewart took on the career-defining role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “ Star Trek: The Next Generation .” As the second major captain of the USS Enterprise, he became the face of “Star Trek” and remained synonymous with the franchise throughout his life. He played the role for seven seasons of “The Next Generation” and went on to reprise it in four films. He notably reprised the role in the final years of his life in “Star Trek: Picard,” a three-season series that caught up with an older version of the character and allowed Stewart to deconstruct his most iconic role.

Stewart’s most notable film role arguably came in the “ X-Men ” franchise, in which he played Professor Charles Xavier. He first took on the role of the mutant superhero team leader in Bryan Singer’s 2000 film “X-Men.” He would continue to play the character for the remainder of his life, appearing in seven films for 20th Century Fox and then bringing the character into the Marvel Cinematic Universe after Disney acquired the IP. Multiverse timelines have allowed him to keep returning even after the character’s ( numerous deaths onscreen; he will next be seen in “ Avengers: Doomsday ” in December.

Stewart’s film and TV success did not deter his stage work, as he continued to lead a variety of Shakespeare and contemporary productions on the New York and London stages for the remainder of his life. He was also an in-demand voice actor, lending his signature baritone to 122 episodes of “American Dad” as well as countless other animated films, shows, and video games.

Throughout his career, Stewart won two Olivier Awards and a Grammy, and received three Primetime Emmy nominations and one Tony Award nomination. He is survived by his wife Sunny Ozell and his two children.

article_text:
Oscar winners and Oscar-nominated filmmakers will be converging on San Francisco for the 12 th edition of Doc Stories, the prestigious nonfiction film festival put on by SFFILM .

The cinematic event running November 5-8 will open with 14 th , Ava DuVernay’s penetrating examination of threats to the protections and rights afforded by the 14 th Amendment. The festival closes with Sam Pollard’s Tutu , a profile of the South African archbishop, anti-Apartheid activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner.

Scroll for the complete lineup of films and talks.

Among other prominent filmmakers heading to Doc Stories: Oscar winner Laura Poitras with her short documentary They’re Here , co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller; two-time Oscar nominee Joshua Oppenheimer with his short film The Revolution Against Death ; three-time Oscar winner Sean Pean with the Ukraine war-themed film he executed produced, Black Sunflowers , and Oscar-shortlisted filmmaker Luke Lorentzen with his latest, Boatbuilders . Two-time Oscar winner Ben Proudfoot will lead a documentary workshop for teen filmmakers.

“For over a decade, Doc Stories has embodied the best of what SFFILM and the San Francisco Bay Area champion and celebrate in new documentary work,” commented Anne Lai , SFFILM’s executive director. “Each film is a wonderful portal into better understanding the world we live in. When daily life can feel quite bruising and fractious, documentaries skillfully encourage us to let our guard down and connect with real-life stories and people… sometimes challenging, often invigorating, and always meaningful. It’s a privilege to bring filmmakers, industry, and audiences—including kids—together for this annual celebration.”

Since 2015, Doc Stories has been the gathering point for the Bay Area’s documentary community, the festival notes, with a program that reliably features standout nonfiction work from around the world. More than two dozen Doc Stories selections have gone on to earn Academy Award nominations, and several have won.

“Curating Doc Stories is one of the great privileges of my job because I get to spend the year seeking out films that I can’t wait to put in front of an audience,” said Jessie Fairbanks , SFFILM’s director of programming. “This year, I found myself drawn to filmmakers who are looking closely at the forces shaping our lives, while also revealing the humor, beauty, resilience, and contradictions within them. These are documentaries I believe deserve to be seen, talked about, and experienced together—and I’m thrilled to share them with our audiences.”

In addition to the public program, SFFILM’s Artist Development team will convene Doc Congress, a day of dialogue and networking for filmmakers, funders, and industry professionals. “This year’s Doc Congress includes a dynamic group discussion on AI use in documentaries featuring Srđan Keča, director of Stanford’s MFA in Documentary Film, and Rachel Antell, co-founder of the Archival Producers Alliance. Artist Development will also host an inaugural Pitch Forum for three local filmmakers. Guest filmmakers will cap off the weekend at Sunday’s annual Doc Stories Brunch.”

From November 2–10, SFFILM’s Education team will host students and teachers at Schools at Doc Stories, with free in-person screenings at SFMOMA, online programs for classrooms nationwide, and conversations with visiting filmmakers that connect to classroom studies and spark curiosity about the wider world.

Doc Stories screenings take place at the Vogue Theatre in San Francisco’s Presidio Heights neighborhood. Below is the program lineup (listed in alphabetical order, with Opening and Closing Night films first and last).

Opening Night: 14th

THU, NOV 5 A T 9:30 PM PT

Ava DuVernay (USA 2026, 107 min)

Ava DuVernay examines the enduring promises of the 14th Amendment through a powerful chorus of voices, joining us in person to discuss this vital new documentary.

All Rivers Spill Their Stories to the Sea

SAT, NOV 7 A T 5:00 PM PT

Jeanie Finlay (UK 2026, 99 min)

When a massive sea life die-off threatens his livelihood, lifelong fisherman Stan Rennie rallies his community in a quest for answers, becoming the unlikeliest of activists.

Black Sunflowers

SAT, NOV 7 A T 8:00 PM PT

James Marcus Haney (Ukraine 2026, 97 min)

Executive produced by Sean Penn, James Marcus Haney’s kinetic, kaleidoscopic portrait of Ukrainian youth is alive with movement, color, and music. Filmed over four years the camera follows artists, drifters, soldiers, and friends as they find pockets of freedom amid mounting uncertainty.

Boatbuilders

SUN, NOV 8 A T 4:30 PM PT

Luke Lorentzen (USA 2026, 103 min)

A visually stunning ode to impeccable craftsmanship and the beauty of Maine, Luke Lorentzen’s latest documentary profiles the workers of Brooklin Boat Yard, a company building custom wooden yachts since 1960.

Citizen Osama

SUN, NOV 8 A T 11:30 AM PT

Ahmed Hassouna (Palestine, France 2026, 71 min)

A photographer turned war reporter documents life in Gaza while raising his newborn son, confronting the impossible challenge of bearing witness to catastrophe while protecting those he loves.

Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been

FRI, NOV 6 A T 8:30 PM PT

Barry Avrich (Canada 2026, 118 min)

The extraordinary singer Darlene Love has lived a big life with its concomitant ups and downs, and this film covers them all as Love herself charts her career, always leading with joy and humor, featuring Cher, David Letterman, Bruce Springsteen, Dionne Warwick, and many more.

Doc Talks: Laura Poitras and Rachel Lauren Mueller

Total Runtime: 60 min

editorial_excerpt_zh: 阿努帕尔娜·罗伊的长片处女作《被遗忘的树木之歌》（2025）曾为她赢得威尼斯电影节地平线单元最佳导演奖。一年后，她带着讲述孟加拉国移民在严酷环境中挣扎求生的剧情片《蓝夜恋人》重返威尼斯……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿努帕尔娜·罗伊的长片处女作《被遗忘的树木之歌》（2025）曾为她赢得威尼斯电影节地平线单元最佳导演奖。一年后，她带着讲述孟加拉国移民在严酷的孟买挣扎求生的剧情片《蓝夜恋人》重返威尼斯。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "罗伊的这部电影采用实景拍摄，以极其华丽的视觉风格处理阶级与性别议题，细腻的运镜支撑起杰出的演员表现。我在釜山国际电影节上采访了罗伊，我们坦诚地探讨了同性恋、审查制度以及她的训练背景。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《电影舞台》：你是如何学习拍电影的？", "translated": true}, true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的主角们经常因为印地语说得不好而受到批评。但我担心自己会错过他们方言之间的区别。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "语言和方言迫使人们以特定的方式行事。我们从显而易见的事开始：印度是一个由欧洲人划分边界的国家。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但如果你向任何方向走30公里，你就会发现一种不同的语言、一种不同的文化。展现内部移民是本片的核心主题。其中一种方式就是展现所有这些不同的语言是如何汇聚在一起的。当人们最终住在同一条街区时，他们的生活便彼此交织。一种生活会影响另一种生活，有时全凭偶然。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在孟买，追寻身份认同是一场持续的挣扎。没有人敢谈论这些问题，因为他们害怕脱离主流工业。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所以你引入了四个主要角色，他们既在努力寻找自己的身份认同，又在寻找向他人呈现这种身份的方式，同时还在努力与他们建立某种联系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这些角色将如何应对？由于被迫和强加的移民，他们失去了起源、失去了根。现在他们背负着过去的记忆。所有人都是如此：卡里姆（Karim）、阿米娜（Ameena）、苏卡（Sukka）、平基（Pinky）。还有奥米（Omi）。奥米原本是一个更深沉、更有层次的角色。他是2002年古吉拉特骚乱的幸存者。我无法把它拍进去，因为我受到了威胁。我的生命受到了威胁。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "印度面临的问题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "印度有很多问题，第三世界的问题。不是P-5的问题。[注：联合国安全理事会五个常任理事国。]", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们来聊聊一些基础的事情。现在的印度电影里，展示性爱场面好像是很酷的事情，你知道吗？不过我告诉你，电影的危机在于电影叙事非常薄弱。我自己也是如此，我是一个叙事讲得很弱的创作者。我们要理解电影是一场挣扎。但我们的传奇影人，比如丽玛·达斯（Rima Das）、南迪塔·达斯（Nandita Das）、米拉·奈尔（Mira Nair）、佐娅·阿赫塔尔（Zoya "text": "当然会有审查压力。但在我的电影里，你只会发现羁绊、爱与友情。我很确信，羁绊、爱与友情不会伤害社会。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们来聊聊你是如何制作《蓝夜恋人》的。制作周期有多长？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们有3个月的前期制作时间。但我写这部电影已经写了3年了。我很早就开始了，在我获得威尼斯奖项之前[《被遗忘的树木之歌》获得威尼斯电影节地平线单元最佳导演奖]。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所以在威尼斯之前，我希望能找到一位制片人，事实也确实如此。说句老实话，维卡斯·库马尔（Vikas Kumar）和来自美国的沙里布·汗（Sharib Khan），这两个人是我职业生涯的顶梁柱。在我去威尼斯之前，他们就跟我签下了《蓝夜恋人》。他们把这部电影拍成了。他们把辛苦赚来的钱投了进去。他们在完全不知道电影能不能上映的情况下冒了险。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所以，回答你的问题，我们有3个月的前期制作，然后是45天的拍摄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Anuparna-ROY-1-800x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "阿努帕尔娜·罗伊", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你们全是在实景地拍摄的吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "酒吧场景除外，那是在摄影棚里拍的。但其他都是真实的外景。海滩附近的真实贫民窟。选景非常艰难。要打破对孟买的刻板印象很难。你一谈到贫民窟，所有的印地语电影展现的就只有达拉维（Dharavi）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我需要找到另一个区域，以便展现观众从未见过的内容。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于那个酒吧，它既是结识女性的夜总会，又是电话色情呼叫中心，男人们在性工作者旁边的房间里。印度真的有这种事吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "没有，这完全是我们虚构出来的。但确实有这样一种呼叫中心，其核心想法是让客户在电话线上停留尽可能长的时间，以增加账单金额。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你有一个精彩的高空俯拍镜头，展露了客户和工作者所在的房间一个又一个地连绵开来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我深知自己没有时间去解释不同的房间，于是我想，为什么不把它们做成一个蒙太奇呢？起初我以为用4个或5个镜头就能展现这个世界。一个人在说话，另一个人在自慰，诸如此类。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但你最后拍成了一个长镜头。这是你和摄影师Debjit Samanta一起琢磨出来的吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我对拍镜头这事非常讲究，因为我觉得自己在这一块比较薄弱。我需要学的东西还很多。出于这种不安全感，每自我写好一场戏，我都会确保自己脑海中已经有了画面。所以大多数镜头在剧本里就已经定好了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你片中那些交通出行的场景——骑摩托车、踏板车、平板卡车、公交车——真的让我印象深刻。你们是怎么规划这些镜头的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "骑车的那个镜头，也就是苏卡（Sukka）初次与卡里姆（Karim）相遇的那个瞬间，很大程度上是受罗伯特·布列松（Robert Bresson）的启发。我以前经常读他的《电影随笔》，看他是如何从小型特写镜头切入的。这真的给了我很大启发。当时我想，“为什么不呢？为什么不呢？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "还有一个长镜头是苏卡在海滩上哭泣，站在水里。卡里姆从他身后走过来。我希望镜头焦距越长越好。卡里姆因为自己的过去不能下水。我们现场即兴发挥了很多。我对摄影师的要求很高，但这始终是一个集体创作的过程。我和Debjit Samanta在《Songs of Forgotten Trees》中也合作过。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你们在街头拍摄时必须取得许可吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这一次我们的资金足够请一位外景经理了。能以那种方式拍电影真是一种特权。没有什么挣扎——只有资金，以及拍出对的镜头。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "能聊聊选角吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "[笑] 哦，这基本上就是裙带关系。普里塔姆·皮拉尼亚（Pritam Pilania，饰演卡里姆）是我的朋友。他是个优秀的演员，所以找他很简单。这帮了我大忙。尼利玛[Sharma，饰演阿米娜（Ameena）]是通过试镜选上的。她的脸一下子就抓住了我的眼球。她有着那种原始而惊艳的面部特征，就像阿米娜一样。我想要一个漂亮的人，因为“美必将伴随毁灭而生”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "布山·辛皮（Bhushan Shimpi，饰演苏卡）曾在我的《Songs of Forgotten Trees》里合作过。找一个充满活力、随时准备做事的人很容易。还有贾廷·萨林（Jatin Sarin，饰演奥米或奥姆兰）也是我的朋友。我当时就知道他极度渴望塑造奥姆兰这样的角色，展现他的挣扎。他是完美的人选，能够承载古吉拉特骚乱带来的所有创伤。删掉他的故事、砍掉他的戏份，这过程实在痛苦。这就是跟朋友一起拍电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你还保留着他的戏份吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的。等政府倒台后，我们会把这些素材拍成一部短片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你能解释一下骚乱是如何影响他的吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "奥姆兰和母亲在2002年离开古吉拉特，此前他的大姐遭到政治暴徒的强奸和杀害。她当时出门去买晚饭吃的羊肉。当母亲找到她的尸体时，尸体已经被切成了像羊肉一样的碎块。当时根本分不清她身上的尸体碎块和她买来的羊肉。现在在孟买，她会买羊肉、做饭，然后把它扔掉。一遍又一遍。我想展现食物带来的创伤，因为这个话题从没人探讨过。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你觉得你是不被允许把它放进电影里吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对，因为他们也会对我和气。我还想活命呢。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为一名导演，你觉得自己不安全吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，因为我在威尼斯谈论了巴勒斯坦。政府不喜欢这样。他们在推特上发了相关言论，然后又删除了。听着，如果你在国际舞台上拿到了麦克风，并且你了解身边的苦难，你还会唱歌吗？每一次他们把麦克风交给我，我都要谈论苦难和令人不适的话题。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所以你不会去拍浪漫喜剧喽？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不，绝不会。但我的下一部电影是浪漫的。它伴随着种族清洗，通过毁灭呈现美。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但在你的电影里，你似乎是一个乐观主义者，相信人们会变好。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对。但我不是社会工作者。作为一名导演，我在拍电影这件事上非常自恋。我正试图将共情的语言融入我的电影中。这并不容易，因为出身特权阶层，去夸大贫苦并把贫困卖给欧洲或美国是件轻而易举的事。明知世界的某一部分正在燃烧，而我们却在这里喝着意式浓缩咖啡，在空调房里聊天。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Lovers in the Blue Night》在2026年釜山国际电影节上进行了展映。", "translated": true}]

A year later she returned to Venice with Lovers in the Blue Night , a drama of Bengali immigrants struggling to survive in a harsh Mumbai."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Shot on location, Roy’s film tackles class and gender issues in a visually opulent style, intimate camerawork supporting exceptional performances. I met with Roy at the Busan International Film Festival, where we had a candid discussion about homosexuality, censorship, and her training."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Film Stage: How did you learn filmmaking?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Anuparna Roy : All my friends were from film schools, and I kind of learned along with them. They kind of taught me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As a Westerner, I couldn’t distinguish among the languages in the film. First, how many languages do you speak?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I only know English, Bengali—the regional Bengali, not the elite Bengali. Also I know Hindi, because I’m forced to know it. And to survive in Bombay, I’m forced to know Marathi."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What languages do you use in the movie?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Three: Jalkau Marathi, again a regional and not elite Marathi. Sylheti Bengali, a very regional Bengali language which is getting wiped out by the so-called elite Bengali languages. Gujarati—there’s a little Gujarati all along. Hindi, of course, because the center of the film is situated in Bombay. So Hindi is used in a very subtle way."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Your lead characters are often criticized because they don’t speak Hindi well. But I’m afraid of missing the distinctions between their dialects."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The languages and dialects force people to act in certain ways. Let’s start with the obvious: India is a country whose borders were created by Europeans."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But if you go 30 kilometers in any direction, you will find a different language, a different culture. Showcasing internal migration is a central theme of the film. One way to do that is to show how all these different languages are coming together. When people end up living in the same lane, their lives become intermingled with each other. One life affects another, sometimes by chance."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Chasing identity is a constant struggle in Bombay. article_text:
Anuparna Roy’s first feature, Songs of Forgotten Trees (2025), won her the Best Director award in the Orizzonti section of the Venice Film Festival. A year later she returned to Venice with Lovers in the Blue Night , a drama of Bengali immigrants struggling to survive in a harsh Mumbai.

Shot on location, Roy’s film tackles class and gender issues in a visually opulent style, intimate camerawork supporting exceptional performances. I met with Roy at the Busan International Film Festival, where we had a candid discussion about homosexuality, censorship, and her training.

The Film Stage: How did you learn filmmaking?

Anuparna Roy : All my friends were from film schools, and I kind of learned along with them. They kind of taught me.

As a Westerner, I couldn’t distinguish among the languages in the film. First, how many languages do you speak?

I only know English, Bengali—the regional Bengali, not the elite Bengali. Also I know Hindi, because I’m forced to know it. And to survive in Bombay, I’m forced to know Marathi.

What languages do you use in the movie?

Three: Jalkau Marathi, again a regional and not elite Marathi. Sylheti Bengali, a very regional Bengali language which is getting wiped out by the so-called elite Bengali languages. Gujarati—there’s a little Gujarati all along. Hindi, of course, because the center of the film is situated in Bombay. So Hindi is used in a very subtle way.

Your lead characters are often criticized because they don’t speak Hindi well. But I’m afraid of missing the distinctions between their dialects.

The languages and dialects force people to act in certain ways. Let’s start with the obvious: India is a country whose borders were created by Europeans.

But if you go 30 kilometers in any direction, you will find a different language, a different culture. Showcasing internal migration is a central theme of the film. One way to do that is to show how all these different languages are coming together. When people end up living in the same lane, their lives become intermingled with each other. One life affects another, sometimes by chance.

Chasing identity is a constant struggle in Bombay. Nobody dares to talk about these problems because they’re afraid to step away from the mainstream industry.

So you introduce four main characters who are both struggling to find their identity, and find a way to present that identity to others. All the while trying to find some sort of connection with them.

How will these characters cope? Due to forced, imposed migration, they lost their origins, their roots. Now they are carrying memories of their past. All of them: Karim, Ameena, Sukka, Pinky. Omi as well. Omi was originally a deeper, more layered character. He is a survivor of the Gujarat Riots in 2002. I couldn’t include that because I had been threatened. My life was under threat.

Problems India faces.

India has many problems, third world problems. Not P-5 problems. [ Note: The five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council. ]

Let’s talk about some basic things. In Indian films nowadays, showcasing sex scenes is something like so cool, you know? I’m telling you though, the crisis of cinema is due to the fact that film narratives are very weak. I put myself in there, I’m a very weak narrative storyteller. It’s a struggle for us to understand cinema. But our legends like Rima Das, Nandita Das, Mira Nair, Zoya Akhtar, Vishal Bhardwaj, Rohan Kanawade, and Tribeny Rai are amazing. For that matter, I’ve learned a lot about craft from Alfonso Cuarón and Joachim Trier. They’ve inspired me a lot.

So, the problems of India… If I start talking about that, the interview will never end, so let’s not do that.

What about the problems with your film? You deal openly with homosexuality—is that an issue that will alarm censorship boards?

Of course there is censorship pressure. But in my films you will find only bonding and love and friendship. I’m pretty sure bonding, love, and friendship will not harm society.

Let’s talk about how you made Lovers . How long was the production?

We had three months for pre-production. But I’ve been writing this film for the past three years. I started long ago, before I won in Venice [ Songs of Forgotten Trees won Best Director in the Orizzonti section of the Venice Film Festival].

So before Venice, I was hoping to get a producer, which is what happened. To be very honest, Vikas Kumar and Sharib Khan, who is from the U.S., these two people are the pillar of my career. They signed me for Lovers in the Blue Night before I went to Venice. They got the film done. They put their hard-earned money into it. They took the risk without ever knowing if the film would come out.

So, to answer your question, we had three months of pre-production and then 45 days of shooting.

Anuparna Roy

Did you shoot everything on location?

Not the bar scenes, they were in a studio. But otherwise real locations. Real slum areas near the beaches. It was a tough location scout. It’s very hard to break the stereotypes about Bombay. You talk about slums and all the Hindi films show is Dharavi.

I needed to find another area in order to show something viewers had never seen before.

About the bar, which is both a nightclub for meeting women and a phone sex call center where the men are in rooms next to the sex workers. Is that something that happens in India?

No, it is a very fictional thing which we made up. But there are call centers where the idea is to keep the clients on the line as long as possible to increase their bills.

You have a wonderful overhead shot where you reveal room after room of client and worker.

I knew I didn’t have time to explain the different rooms, so I thought why not do a montage of them? At first I thought four or five shots to show this world. One guy is talking, another is masturbating, and so on.

You did it in one take instead. Is that something you worked out with your cinematographer Debjit Samanta?

I’m very particular when it comes to taking shots because I feel I’m weak in that area. I need to learn a lot. Out of that insecurity, whenever I write a scene, I make sure how I’m seeing it. So most of the shots are in the script already.

I was really impressed with your transit scenes, on bikes and scooters, flatbed trucks, buses. How did you plan them?

The bike shot, the moment when Sukka first meets Karim, was pretty much inspired by Robert Bresson. I used to read his Notes on the Cinematographer a lot and how he used to start with small, close shots. That really inspired me. I’m like, “Why not? Why not?”

There’s another long shot of Sukkah crying at the beach, standing in the water. Karim comes up behind him. I wanted it to be as long a lens as possible. Karim can’t go in the water because of his past. We improvised a lot. I ask a lot from the cinematographer, but it’s always a collaborative effort. Debjit Samanta and I also worked together on Songs of Forgotten Trees.

Did you have to get permission to shoot on the streets?

This time we had enough money for a location manager. It was a privilege to shoot that way. No struggle—just money and just getting the right shot.

Can you talk about casting?

[Laughing] Oh, it was pretty much nepotism. Pritam Pilania (Karim) is my friend. He’s a great actor, so hiring him was easy. So that helped me a lot. Casting Neelima [Sharma, who plays Ameena) was through an audition. Her face really grabbed my attention. She had these raw, amazing features, just like Ameena. I wanted someone who was pretty, because “beauty shall come with destruction.”

Bhushan Shimpi (Sukka) worked with me in Songs of Forgotten Trees . It’s easy to hire someone who’s vibrant and ready to do things. And Jatin Sarin, Omi or Omran, is also my friend. I knew that he desperate to portray a character like Omran, to show his struggle. He was the perfect choice, able to carry all the trauma of the Gujarat riots. It was painful to remove his story, to chop out his scenes. This was making a film with friends.

You still have his scenes?

Yes. We’ll turn them into a short once the government’s gone.

Can you explain how the riots affected him?

Omran and his mother left Gujarat in 2002 after his elder sister was raped and murdered by political goons. She had gone outside to buy mutton for dinner. When his mother found her dead body, it had been chopped into pieces like mutton. It was very hard to differentiate the pieces of her body from the mutton she had purchased. Now in Bombay, she buys mutton, cooks it, and throws it out. Over and over. I wanted to show food trauma because it’s never discussed.

You felt you weren’t allowed to include it in the film?

No, because they’d do the same thing to me. I want to live.

Do you feel unsafe as a director?

Yes, because I talked about Palestine at Venice. The government didn’t like it. They tweeted about it, and then deleted the tweet. Listen, if you’re given a mic on an international stage and you are aware about the miseries around you, will you sing a song? Every time they give me a mic, I’ll talk about miseries and uncomfortable topics.

So you’re not going to make a rom-com?

No, never. But my next film is romantic. It comes with ethnic cleansing, beauty through destruction.

But in your films you seem to be an optimist, to believe that people can get better.

Yeah. But I’m not a social worker. I’m very narcissistic in terms of making films as a director. The language of empathy is something I’m trying to bring into my films. It’s not easy because coming from a privileged background, it’s easy to emphasize poverty and sell poverty to Europe or America. Knowing that a portion of the world is burning and we are having espresso here, talking in an air-conditioned room.

Lovers in the Blue Night screened at the 2026 Busan International Film Festival.

article_text:
The summer was a turning point for Phillips , with several leaders leaving the auction house, including Miety Heiden , chairman of private sales, and Jonathan Crocket , chairman for Asia. While reporting at the time showed that Phillips was pivoting strategy after a costly attempt to compete with Sotheby’s and Christie’s, a new filing adds some financial figures to the picture.

According to the auction house’s 2025 filing with Companies House, the UK government agency that keeps annual records for companies registered in the country, Phillips’s turnover fell 22.3 percent, from $44.13 million (£33.18 million) in 2024 to $34.26 million (£25.76 million) in 2025. Its pre-tax loss, however, narrowed to $14.02 million (£10.54 million), from $61.86 million (£46.51 million) the previous year, when results were weighed down by a one-time, non-cash charge of about $35.9 million (£27 million) tied to the revaluation of balances with other Phillips entities. Gross profit fell 6 percent, to $19.57 million (£14.72 million) from $20.86 million (£15.68 million).

The filing covers Phillips’s UK accounts only, not its operations in the US, Europe, or Asia. The auction house, which is owned by the Russian luxury retailer Mercury Group, has headquarters in London and New York.

“Phillips is a global business, operating across the United States, Europe, and Asia. The accounts filed at Companies House relate to only certain elements of our international operations and do not reflect the financial performance of Phillips as a whole or how the business is performing today,” a Phillips spokesperson told ARTnews , adding that they expect 2026 to be one of the most successful years in Phillips’ history through a combination of a focused strategy and strong commercial performance.

The spokesperson said that the auction house continues to be committed to the top end of the market, unscored by its fall auction season and welcoming new collectors through “other important sectors.” “This follows a strong 2025, when global sales increased by 10 percent and private sales grew by 66 percent,” said the spokesperson. “That momentum has continued throughout 2026, reflecting the strength of our strategy and the confidence of our clients in Phillips.” A prominent former Phillips employee, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said that the auction house is introducing handbags into its categories.

In 2025, Phillips held 23 auctions in London, four fewer than the previous year. In the filing, the company said it earns commissions by facilitating the sale of art, design, photography, editions, watches, and jewelry, either at auction or privately. Aggregate UK auction sales totaled $122.6 million (£92.2 million) in 2025, down 31.3 percent from $178.6 million (£134.3 million) in 2024. That figure represents the hammer price of property sold at auction plus buyer’s premium. Phillips also recorded $39.6 million (£29.8 million) in private treaty sales for 2025, a 23.1 percent increase from $32.2 million (£24.2 million) in 2024. According to the filing, private treaty sales represent the gross value of sales made outside of auction.

Phillips said in the filing that the group’s “operating results and liquidity” are significantly influenced by a “number of key factors.”They include the “overall strength of the various worldwide economies and financial markets,” “foreign currency exchange rate movements,” the “importance of proper authentication and/or validation of provenance,” and “competition with other auctioneers and with art dealers.” Other factors include the demand for art, the resources needed for proper know-your-customer (KYC) checks to prevent money laundering, and “continued support from the group’s ultimate controlling party.”

The filing notes that the group and company have “historically been loss making and are in a net liability position at the reporting date.” The directors said they have received written confirmation from Phillips’s ultimate parent company, Mercury Group Trading Limited, that it intends to continue providing “financial support” and has “confirmed that they have the financial resources” to do so. However, the filing also says Phillips remains reliant on its ultimate beneficial owners, whose support “cannot be guaranteed.” The directors and the auditor both flagged this as a “material uncertainty” that “may cast significant doubt” on the group’s ability to continue as a going concern.

The directors who served during 2025 were former chief executive Ed Dolman, who resigned as a director on June 7, 2025; Paul de Bono, chief operating officer for Europe; and chief financial officer Annette Schwaer, who resigned on August 19, 2026. CEO Martin Wilson was appointed a director the same day.
